results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 47 aligned outline summaries state the controlling idea of their spec paragraph, in spec order; the three callout units match no spec paragraph. The summary of Asking for the Promise ¶1 names the section overview as well as the final-versus-estimated definition, and the second half is p22's idea.

One unit was marked two_ideas (Asking for the Promise ¶1). Its overview sentences carry the section transition the spec declares at that position (/sections/4/transition_in: time as the first change, the merchant's choices and the reversal as the second); the unit's own controlling idea is p22's single contrast of the default final authorization with the estimate. The spec's idea for p22 is not double.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: scene and no-answer units to S5, the definition units to S1, the decline units (including the soft/hard shorthand) to S2, the window units to S3, the variants and initiator units to S4, the public-record and comparison units to S6, and the Larkfield payments to S1, S2, S3 and S5.

Each spec evidence item appears and is tied to a statement of what it shows: quotations are followed or framed by the author's reading (for example 'So the decision is made on the issuer's side of the network'), every table has a lead-in or closing sentence saying what it sets out, and the three figures carry captions that state what they show. The miscount in the sentence that introduces the promise table is recorded under flow_is_followable.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: A Timeout on the First of the Month ¶1
results.quote: On the first of each month Larkfield attempts **38%** of its monthly membership volume in a **6-hour** window.
results.finding: The spec declares a sentence at the start of the scene that presents the incident as an example of the introduction's claim that an approval can exist without the merchant knowing. The section opens on a volume statistic and re-identifies the incident only by its date; the claim is not picked up until the second paragraph ('The members' banks had approved the first requests'), and flow reader B (item 3.1) wondered whether this was a different incident from the one the introduction told.

results.draft_locus: Who Is Asking: Customer-Initiated, Merchant-Initiated and Stored Credentials ¶1
results.quote: Two labels in the validity table were only glossed.
results.finding: Both flow readers could not say why this section comes after the variants and not before the validity windows (reader A: 'Partly unclear'; reader B: 'unclear'), both read its opening as the repair of a forward reference and not as a step in the argument, and both put moving it ahead of the validity section first among their reorderings. The difficulty comes from the declared order: the validity section needs the two labels two sections before they are defined. The spec's rationale (the reader needs both uses of the label first) is not what either reader experienced, and the spec's open_questions already records the same flow-rubric note as not acted on, so the decision is the author's.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, section 2 item 7 and section 4 item 1 (same point as flow reader A, section 2 item 7, section 3 items 7 and 13, section 4 item 1)

results.draft_locus: A Promise with an Expiry Date: Validity Windows ¶3
results.quote: which row of the table applies is not settled by your API parameters alone
results.finding: Both flow readers re-read this sentence: it has two colons and joins where to read the expiry with who classifies the payment, 'the table' is ambiguous after two tables (Visa's and the provider one), and it states that classification can be in doubt without saying why. Splitting the sentence, naming Visa's table and adding one clause on why the classification can differ from what was sent would fix it within the unit.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.9 (same passage as flow reader A, section 3 item 8)

results.draft_locus: The Issuer Decides, and Mostly Does Not Say Why ¶3
results.quote: Adyen's page on these categories says 15 retries in 30 days where the rule text says 20
results.finding: The discrepancy with Adyen's page is stated before the reader has been given Visa's limit of 20 attempts in 30 days, which appears only in the table after the paragraph. Reader A did not know what '20' referred to; reader B read on to the table and came back.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.6 (same passage as flow reader A, section 3 item 5)

results.draft_locus: When No Answer Comes Back: Unknown Outcomes and Stand-In Processing ¶3
results.finding: The pronoun depends on the last sentence of the previous paragraph ('The payment is an object you can fetch.'). Across the paragraph break both readers first took 'it' for the way out or the idempotency key and had to look back. Naming the subject ('On Adyen the payment cannot be fetched') removes the stumble.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3.11 (same passage as flow reader A, section 3 item 14)

results.draft_locus: What an Authorization Is: A Message, a Decision and a Hold ¶5
results.quote: the table sets the one promise against these four
results.finding: The sentence announces one promise and four things not promised; the table has three rows on each side, and the fourth non-promise ('that the promise lasts') appears as a left-hand row. Flow reader A (item 4) counted twice. Reported by one reader only.

results.draft_locus: A Promise with an Expiry Date: Validity Windows ¶4
results.quote: Visa's rules list that right as Dispute Condition 11.3.
results.finding: Flow reader A (item 9) re-read the preceding list of four quoted fragments with two inserted definitions, and 'that right' has no antecedent: only a chargeback has been named. Reported by one reader only.

results.draft_locus: Asking for the Promise: Five Variants and When Each Fits ¶6
results.quote: | Estimate with increments | The final amount is unknown: a stay, a rental |
results.finding: Flow reader B (item 3.7) re-read to match the five rows of the design table to the five ways of asking announced at the top of the section and could not: the table splits the exact amount in two, merges estimate and increment, and has no reversal row. A clause saying that the table regroups the variants as designs would settle it. Reported by one reader only.

results.draft_locus: When No Answer Comes Back: Unknown Outcomes and Stand-In Processing ¶4
results.quote: Where the network cannot stand in, the code is 91
results.finding: Code 91 was glossed in the decline-category table as 'issuer or switch inoperative' and is glossed here as 'time-out when no stand-in' without a link between the two; flow reader A (item 16) went back to the table to confirm it was the same code. Reported by one reader only.

Each term AC-4 lists is given a plain clause at or before the point the argument relies on it: hold ('it lowers the amount the cardholder can spend by the approved amount, without debiting the account'), response code ('a two-character code in the response message'), the window ('a maximum number of calendar days to process the transaction'), estimated, incremental, partial and zero-value authorization and reversal at first use in their own paragraphs, customer- and merchant-initiated glossed before the validity table ('the cardholder, taking part at the checkout, or the merchant, charging a stored card alone') and defined in Who Is Asking, stored credential defined there, and stand-in processing glossed where the first table names it ('The network can answer for an unavailable or slow issuer'). Terms the flow readers met unexplained (idempotency key, acquirer, capture, 3-D Secure, Keel and K1, K2, K5, Studio Noord) are in the audience's already_knows through the earlier pages (meet-larkfield's Keel table, journey-of-a-payment). 'Estimated authorization' and 'extended Authorization indicator' occur in rows of the Visa table before or without a definition; the argument does not rely on those rows and neither flow reader reported them.
The introduction opens on a dated incident with its cost, states the thesis in the second paragraph, places the chapter on the journey and gives a roadmap; it is none of the weak patterns.

The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic or body evidence, and does not end on a rephrased thesis alone: it sorts what holds by how settled it is, gives the author's synthesis and a course of action, and hands off to the next chapter.

The synthesis is stated and no single section states it ('your copy of the answer can be vague, stale or missing. The remedy is always to go back to a record closer to the issuer before acting.'), and the so-what follows ('A payment record with one status field cannot hold a promise', 'cheaper than 1,840 refunds').

The conclusion returns to the 1,840 members of 1 November 2026 as the spec's callback describes: 'each first request had already obtained a promise, and the renewal job needed a third outcome, the same key and a question to the provider before it sent anything new.'

From the introduction alone the reader predicted all nine body sections in the roadmap's order, the three kinds of evidence (the Larkfield case, network rules and codes, provider behavior side by side) and the instructional second-person tone. The reader noted that the introduction says little about what the 'ways to ask' and 'who is asking' sections argue, and guessed both correctly.

The cold reader says the shop cannot know the outcome ('the bank may have approved the €45 and placed a hold'), records it as unknown, resolves the first request by same-key retry, lookup at the provider or cancel by its own reference, and sends a new request only when the first is known to have failed. Every element of the expected answer is present.

The cold reader says the insufficient-funds decline (code 51, Category 2) may be retried within 20 attempts in 30 days and the Category 1 decline must never be resubmitted, takes the category from the network's code and retry advice and not from the provider's reason, and names the cost: Visa's system integrity fees, blocked attempts and issuers reading retries as fraud.

Windows carry source and date (Visa Table 5-11 and Table 7-2, 24 October 2026; Stripe and Adyen 'n.d., accessed November 2026'); the retry limit of 20 in 30 days is quoted from Table 7-2 and Adyen's 15 is attributed to Adyen's page; Mastercard figures are attributed to the providers ('By Adyen's documentation, Mastercard returns a separate Merchant Advice Code', 'For Mastercard, whose rules I could not read, both providers report 7 days'); the 7-day versus 10-day difference is stated without a cause ('Stripe's page gives no reason, and I will not supply one').
